items.title: If something grows at 3% per year, it doubles in 23 years
items.claim: Compound growth at rate r% has a fixed doubling time of about 70/r years (rule of 70) or 72/r (rule of 72). The doubling time doesn't change as the quantity grows. That's what 'exponential' means — proportional rate, not larger jumps.
items.prompt: Why is the doubling time constant?

options.text: For exponential growth dN/dt = kN, N(t) = N0 * e^(kt). Doubling time T = ln(2)/k ≈ 0.693/k. Independent of N0 — the time to go from 1 to 2 equals the time to go from 1000 to 2000
Only applies to populations of bacteria

items.reveal:
Exponential growth: dN/dt = k * N. Solution: N(t) = N_0 e^(kt). Doubling time T = ln(2)/k.

Rule of 70/72: if k% per period, doubling time ≈ 70/k (or 72/k) periods. At 7%/year, doubles in ~10 years. At 1%/year, doubles in ~70 years. At 0.5%/year (current global population growth), doubles in ~140 years.

Exponential growth is unrealistic for long times — no real system maintains constant growth rate forever. The logistic model corrects: dN/dt = k * N * (1 - N/K), where K is the carrying capacity.

Logistic solution: N(t) = K / (1 + ((K - N_0)/N_0) * e^(-kt)). Starts exponential (when N << K), saturates at K.

Applications:
- Epidemics: early growth (susceptible >> infected) is exponential; saturates as susceptibles deplete (or interventions take effect). The famous 'flatten the curve' is intervening in this growth equation.
- Populations: many wild populations roughly logistic. Carrying capacity set by food, predation, disease.
- Innovation diffusion: technology adoption (smartphones, electric cars) often logistic.
- Tumour growth: early stages can be exponential; later stages limited by blood supply.

Misinterpretations:
- 'Exponential' is loosely used to mean 'fast growth'. Mathematically, it means proportional growth. A linear quantity can grow faster than an exponential one in the short term.
- Confusing exponential growth (rate proportional to value) with super-exponential (faster than any fixed exponential).
- Underestimating doubling times. Many people fail the 'penny doubling' problem: a penny doubled daily for 30 days becomes ~10 million dollars.
items.why: Exponential growth feels like 'fast growth'. Mathematically it's something specific: constant percentage rate, constant doubling time. Understanding doubling times is key to understanding epidemics, populations, finance, and Moore's law.

items.title: Compounding interest infinitely fast gives the same answer as compounding once
items.claim: Invest 1 dollar at 100 percent annual interest. Compounded once a year: 2 dollars. Twice: 2.25. Monthly: 2.61. Continuously: 2.71828... — the constant e. Not infinity, not 2 — a specific irrational number.
items.prompt: Why does compounding infinitely often give a finite limit?

options.text: (1 + 1/n) to the power n is bounded above by 3 for all n, and increases monotonically; its limit as n approaches infinity is e, a fundamental constant of growth
Each compounding adds tiny amounts that cancel each other
Math caps results at e by definition

items.reveal:
Jacob Bernoulli, investigating compound interest, asked what happens as compounding frequency goes to infinity. He calculated (1 + 1/n) to the power n for ever-larger n and found the values approached a specific number between 2.71 and 2.72.

The number is e — base of the natural logarithm. It shows up everywhere: continuous growth (e to the rt), the normal distribution (Gauss), Euler's identity (e to the i pi equals minus 1), derangements in combinatorics, and the most-common-digit problem (Benford's law).

e can be characterised many ways:
- Limit of (1 + 1/n) to the power n.
- Infinite sum 1 + 1/1! + 1/2! + 1/3! + ...
- Unique number whose exponential function equals its own derivative.

Like pi, e is transcendental — no polynomial with rational coefficients has e as a root.
items.why: Compounding 'more often' sounds like it should produce ever-larger returns. The limit is finite because each compounding period adds proportionally less.

items.title: Compound interest of 7% turns 100 into 14,974 over 75 years
items.claim: Simple interest at 7% for 75 years: 100 + (75 x 7) = 625. Compound interest at 7% for 75 years: 100 x 1.07^75 = 14,974. The same rate, the same time. Compounding multiplies the result by 24x.
items.prompt: Why does compound interest diverge so dramatically?

options.text: Compound interest grows exponentially (multiplicatively each period); simple interest grows linearly (additively). Over long horizons, exponential growth always vastly exceeds linear, no matter the rate
The two are basically the same after enough time
Compound interest only works for whole-year periods

items.reveal_title: The rule of 72 and the magic of compounding
items.reveal:
Compound interest: each period, interest is paid on (principal + accumulated interest). Mathematically: A = P (1 + r)^n.
Simple interest: A = P (1 + r * n).

Rule of 72: at compound rate r% per year, money doubles in about 72/r years. At 7%, doubling time ~10.3 years. In 75 years that's ~7 doublings, so ~128x the original.

Applied historically: Einstein supposedly called compound interest 'the eighth wonder of the world' (apocryphal but illustrative). It explains:
- Why starting to save in your 20s vs your 40s makes such a huge difference.
- Why credit card debt at 20% APR explodes if minimum payments are made.
- Why long-run stock returns (averaging ~7% real) translate into vast wealth over careers.

For short horizons (1-2 periods), compound and simple interest are nearly equal. For long horizons, the gap is enormous. The gap is the 'magic' that financial planners try to communicate to young people, often unsuccessfully.

Negative compounding (decay) works the same way: 7% inflation halves purchasing power in ~10 years.
items.why: Linear and exponential are taught as adjacent concepts. They diverge in practice so dramatically that human intuition completely fails for long horizons. Anyone making long-term financial decisions needs to feel this in their bones.
